cards.text: This psalm doesn't give us a writer's name, and it doesn't warm up either. No small talk, no 'testing, testing, is this thing on.' The writer opens at FULL volume about the LORD: 'The LORD reigns!'

cards.question: The LORD reigns, and the writer says He's dressed like a King. What is the LORD robed in?
The LORD's robe isn't the only thing He has on. He has clothed and armed Himself with ___.
Then the writer turns to the world itself. He says the world is firmly established and cannot be moved.

cards.text: Now the writer switches it up. He turns and talks right to the LORD Himself.

cards.question: The writer tells the LORD that His throne was established only recently.
The LORD's throne goes way back, and so does He. The writer tells the LORD that He is from all ___.

cards.text: Then the psalm gets LOUD. Something starts rising, and the writer tells the LORD all about it.

cards.question: What does the writer tell the LORD has risen?

cards.text: And it keeps coming. The rivers raise their voice, and the seas lift up their pounding waves, like a group chat at 6 a.m. where one buzz turns into ten and the phone rattles right off the counter.

cards.question: All that water is roaring and crashing. Where does the writer say the LORD is?
The mighty breakers of the sea are pounding away, but the writer says the LORD on high is ___.

cards.text: Last verse. The writer's done with the waves, and now he talks to the LORD about His testimonies and His house.

cards.question: The writer says the LORD's testimonies still need to be proven.
What does the writer say adorns the LORD's house?
The writer says holiness adorns the LORD's house for all the days to come.

findings.problem: The question asks what the LORD is robed in, with Majesty, Light and Righteousness as answers. All three are believable things for God to be clothed in elsewhere in Scripture, and nothing on the earlier cards helps the baker reason toward majesty. 'Dressed like a King' fits all three. This is the same pattern as the bad Psalm 23 example 'What does He anoint David's head with?', which guesses a wording detail.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The question asks what adorns the LORD's house, with Holiness, Gold and Cedar as answers. Card 13 only says the writer talks about His house. Nothing before this card lets the baker reason toward holiness over gold or cedar, which are both real temple materials (1 Kings 6). The baker can only guess or get lucky.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Almost every choice card tests a wording detail of a line: robed in, armed with, from all ___, has risen, is ___, adorns. No card asks about the psalm's movement or meaning. The central picture is that the waters rise and roar, yet the LORD on high is majestic above them. No card asks what that contrast shows, or why the writer moves from the roaring waters to the LORD's sure testimonies and holy house. Several cards could be reworked into questions about the picture and the turn.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's voice is thin through most of the walkthrough. Card 10's group chat line is the only real joke. Cards 5, 8 and 13 are plain transitions ('Now the writer switches it up.' 'Last verse.') that read like a pleasant narrator rather than a laugh-out-loud storyteller. Moments like the waters lifting their voice or the throne being established long ago could hold a real laugh without muddying a fact.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
